original_question: If global-in-time solutions of the evolutionary incompressible Jeffreys-type viscoelastic fluid problem can be constructed, can one then build generalized attractors and/or inertial manifolds for that problem?
target_in_paper: Section 3, in the review paragraph on the boundary-value problem with the full material derivative, i.e. equations (0.2), (0.4), (0.5), (2.15): the paper says that global-in-time weak solvability is known, uniqueness is open, and a global attractor has already been constructed for the autonomous problem by using the theory of minimal trajectory attractors; the nonautonomous analogue is a uniform attractor.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies that the relevant issue is long-time dynamics for an evolutionary incompressible Jeffreys-type viscoelastic fluid problem, and that some attractor notion is the right asymptotic object once global-in-time solvability is available. It also correctly gestures toward the fact that ordinary dynamical-systems attractors are problematic here because uniqueness is not available, so a generalized/trajectory-type attractor framework is the natural one.
missing_details: The paper is not speaking about an unspecified 'Jeffreys-type problem' in general, but specifically about the bounded-domain initial-boundary value problem with incompressibility (0.2), momentum equation (0.4), no-slip boundary condition (0.5), and constitutive law with the full material derivative (2.15).
The relevant solutions in the paper are global weak solutions, not arbitrary 'global-in-time solutions' without specifying weak/strong class.
The paper keeps track of prescribed initial velocity and initial stress; your draft omits both.
The autonomous/nonautonomous distinction matters: the paper discusses a global attractor in the autonomous case and a uniform attractor in the nonautonomous case.
The paper emphasizes that uniqueness of weak solutions is open; this is why a minimal trajectory-attractor construction is needed. Your draft does not mention this obstruction.
The paper also notes the lack of the invariant dissipative estimates required by the classical attractor approach; this is part of the motivation for the generalized attractor framework.

The attractor statement is not posed conditionally in the paper for this full-derivative problem: the review reports that the attractor construction has already been carried out once global weak solvability is known.
Your draft adds 'inertial manifolds,' but the paper passage closest to your draft does not mention inertial manifolds.

The paper's 'generalized attractor' content is more faithfully rendered as trajectory/global attractors via the theory of minimal trajectory attractors, and uniform attractors in the nonautonomous case.
The forcing term is assumed autonomous when discussing the stationary weak solution and the associated global attractor; that hypothesis is hidden in your draft.
refined_question: For the autonomous initial-boundary value problem for an incompressible Jeffreys-type viscoelastic medium in a bounded domain, given by the incompressibility condition (0.2), momentum equation (0.4), no-slip boundary condition (0.5), and constitutive relation with the full material derivative (2.15), with prescribed initial velocity and initial stress, can one construct a global attractor for the class of global weak solutions despite the lack of uniqueness and the failure of the classical invariant-dissipative semigroup approach, by using the framework of minimal trajectory attractors; and, in the nonautonomous case, can one analogously construct a uniform attractor?
justification: The nearest paper-faithful target is not an open inertial-manifold problem. In Section 3 the review explicitly singles out the boundary-value problem with the full derivative (0.2), (0.4), (0.5), (2.15), says that global weak solvability is especially important there, notes that uniqueness is not proved, and then states that a global attractor for this problem was constructed by a specially developed theory of minimal trajectory attractors, precisely because the classical approach breaks down without uniqueness and invariant dissipative estimates. The same paragraph says these attractor results extend to the nonautonomous case. So the draft is only partially aligned with the paper: it points toward asymptotic objects after global solvability, but it is too vague about the model, omits the weak-solution and nonuniqueness framework, and is not paper-faithful in adding inertial manifolds or in treating the attractor construction as merely hypothetical for this specific problem.
